items.stem: Which is an example of a habitat?
items.answer: a mangrove swamp on the coast of Kenya
items.markingKey: a mangrove swamp on the coast of Kenya. A place where organisms live.

items.stem: Explain the difference between niche and habitat.
items.answer: A habitat is the place where an organism lives; its niche is its role in the ecosystem, including all its interactions with biotic and abiotic factors.
items.markingKey: A habitat is the place where an organism lives; its niche is its role in the ecosystem, including all its interactions with biotic and abiotic factors. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Animals develop adaptations during their lifetime because they need them." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Adaptations arise by natural selection on heritable variation over generations; individuals do not develop them in response to need.
items.markingKey: Adaptations arise by natural selection on heritable variation over generations; individuals do not develop them in response to need. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Marram grass grows on mobile sand dunes and has very deep roots and rhizomes. Which pair of abiotic factors are these adaptations most likely to address?
options: low water availability and shifting sand
items.answer: low water availability and shifting sand
items.markingKey: A. Roots reach water; rhizomes resist burial.

items.stem: Describe adaptations of named organisms to their habitats and explain how abiotic factors limit species distribution.
items.answer: Marram grass: rolled leaves, sunken stomata, hairs, deep roots, rhizomes. Mangroves: pneumatophores, prop roots, salt glands. Range of tolerance; limiting factors; zones of stress and intolerance; biotic factors modify.
items.markingKey: Marram grass: rolled leaves, sunken stomata, hairs, deep roots, rhizomes. Mangroves: pneumatophores, prop roots, salt glands. Range of tolerance; limiting factors; zones of stress and intolerance; biotic factors modify.

items.stem: Define the term "xerophyte".
items.answer: A plant adapted to survive in dry conditions with little water
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a plant adapted to survive in dry conditions with little water. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why do mangrove leaves often have salt glands?
options: To excrete excess salt absorbed from seawater.
items.answer: To excrete excess salt absorbed from seawater.
items.markingKey: A. Maintains water potential and prevents toxicity.

items.stem: Explain how mangroves are adapted to life in coastal saline swamps.
items.answer: Pneumatophores (aerial roots) allow gas exchange in anaerobic mud; prop roots give stability in soft sediment; salt glands excrete salt and ultrafiltration at roots excludes it; viviparous seedlings establish quickly.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Pneumatophores (aerial roots) allow gas exchange in anaerobic mud; prop roots give stability in soft sediment; salt glands excrete salt and ultrafiltration at roots excludes it; viviparous seedlings establish quickly. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

A belt transect was set up from the woodland edge into a field. At 5 m intervals a 1 m² quadrat was used to estimate the percentage cover of bracken (Pteridium aquilinum), and light intensity was measured.

Briefly describe marram grass (Ammophila arenaria) on European sand dunes and explain what it reveals about adaptations to a habitat.
items.answer: It stabilises mobile dunes, rolling its leaves in dry weather and growing up through accumulating sand. Rolled leaves reduce transpiration and rhizomes allow survival of burial – heritable features suited to the abiotic conditions of dunes.
items.markingKey: Context (It stabilises mobile dunes, rolling its leaves in dry weather and growing up through accumulating sand.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: "Abiotic factors are more important than biotic factors in determining the distribution of species." Discuss.
items.answer: Abiotic factors determine where species could live (fundamental range), but biotic interactions often determine where they actually live.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: abiotic factors set the limits of tolerance (e.g. temperature limits of corals); biome patterns follow temperature and rainfall. Arguments against: competition, predation and disease often limit species within physically suitable areas; mutualists such as pollinators are needed for many plants. Supported judgement: Abiotic factors determine where species could live (fundamental range), but biotic interactions often determine where they actually live. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "zonation"?
options: The consumption of plants or plant parts by animals
The percentage of the area of a quadrat occupied by a particular species
The range of values of an abiotic factor within which a species can survive, with an optimum range in which it thrives
The gradual change in distribution of species across a habitat in response to an environmental gradient, such as on a rocky shore
items.answer: The gradual change in distribution of species across a habitat in response to an environmental gradient, such as on a rocky shore
items.markingKey: D. "zonation" is the gradual change in distribution of species across a habitat in response to an environmental gradient, such as on a rocky shore.

items.stem: Maya writes: "The optimum range of tolerance is always at the edge of a species’ distribution." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The optimum is usually in the middle of the range; populations at the edges are under physiological stress.
items.markingKey: The optimum is usually in the middle of the range; populations at the edges are under physiological stress. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why are transects used rather than random quadrats when studying zonation?
options: Transects sample systematically along an environmental gradient, showing how distribution changes.
items.answer: Transects sample systematically along an environmental gradient, showing how distribution changes.
items.markingKey: A. Systematic sampling along the gradient.

items.answer: 48.5 per m²; about 2425

items.stem: A climograph shows monthly temperatures 25–28 °C all year and rainfall over 200 mm every month. Which biome is it?
items.answer: tropical rainforest
items.markingKey: B. Hot and wet all year.

items.stem: Describe how the distribution of species can be investigated using transects and explain how range of tolerance and climate determine distribution.
items.answer: Transect method: tape, quadrats at intervals, percentage cover, abiotic measurements (light meter, soil probe), correlation; range of tolerance curve (optimum, stress, intolerance); biomes by temperature and rainfall; climographs; examples.
items.markingKey: Transect method: tape, quadrats at intervals, percentage cover, abiotic measurements (light meter, soil probe), correlation; range of tolerance curve (optimum, stress, intolerance); biomes by temperature and rainfall; climographs; examples.

items.stem: Which biome is characterised by permafrost, low temperatures and low-growing vegetation?
items.answer: tundra
items.markingKey: A. Short growing season.

items.stem: Distinguish between tropical rainforest and temperate deciduous forest.
items.answer: Tropical rainforest is hot and wet all year with very high diversity and evergreen trees; temperate deciduous forest has distinct seasons with trees shedding leaves in winter and lower diversity.
items.markingKey: Tropical rainforest is hot and wet all year with very high diversity and evergreen trees; temperate deciduous forest has distinct seasons with trees shedding leaves in winter and lower diversity. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how a transect can be used to investigate the effect of an abiotic factor on the distribution of a species.
items.answer: Lay a tape across the gradient (e.g. from shore to cliff); place quadrats at regular intervals; record abundance (percentage cover or counts) and measure the abiotic factor at each point; plot both and test for correlation (e.g. Spearman’s).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Lay a tape across the gradient (e.g. from shore to cliff); place quadrats at regular intervals; record abundance (percentage cover or counts) and measure the abiotic factor at each point; plot both and test for correlation (e.g. Spearman’s). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which zonation on a rocky shore in Cape Town shows the use of transects to study distribution.
items.answer: From low to high tide line, kelp, mussels, limpets, barnacles and periwinkles occur in distinct bands. A transect up the shore reveals how tolerance of exposure and desiccation determines each species’ zone.
items.markingKey: Context (From low to high tide line, kelp, mussels, limpets, barnacles and periwinkles occur in distinct bands.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A transect up the shore reveals how tolerance of exposure and desiccation determines each species’ zone. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the use of transects to study distribution.

items.stem: Using coral reefs and sea temperature as an example, explain range of tolerance.
items.answer: Reef-building corals live mainly between 23 and 29 °C; above about 30 °C they bleach. Temperature outside the optimum stresses corals, limiting their distribution to warm, shallow tropical seas.
items.markingKey: Context (Reef-building corals live mainly between 23 and 29 °C; above about 30 °C they bleach.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Temperature outside the optimum stresses corals, limiting their distribution to warm, shallow tropical seas. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to range of tolerance.

items.stem: "Transects are the most effective way to study species distribution in a habitat." Discuss.
items.answer: Transects are best for gradients; other methods (random quadrats, mark–recapture, eDNA) suit other questions.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they reveal patterns along environmental gradients; they are simple and repeatable. Arguments against: they may miss species between sampling points; random sampling is better for estimating population size where there is no gradient. Supported judgement: Transects are best for gradients; other methods (random quadrats, mark–recapture, eDNA) suit other questions. items.stem: Define the term "obligate anaerobe".
items.answer: An organism that can only survive in the absence of oxygen, for which oxygen is toxic
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an organism that can only survive in the absence of oxygen, for which oxygen is toxic. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why can no two species occupy exactly the same niche indefinitely?
options: One would outcompete the other for the same resources (competitive exclusion).
items.answer: One would outcompete the other for the same resources (competitive exclusion).
items.markingKey: A. Gause’s principle.

items.stem: Distinguish between holozoic nutrition and saprotrophic nutrition.
items.answer: Holozoic organisms ingest food and digest it internally (e.g. animals); saprotrophs secrete enzymes onto dead matter and absorb the products externally (e.g. fungi).
items.markingKey: Holozoic organisms ingest food and digest it internally (e.g. animals); saprotrophs secrete enzymes onto dead matter and absorb the products externally (e.g. fungi). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to methanogenic archaea in the rumen of cattle, explain how it illustrates obligate anaerobic metabolism.
items.answer: Archaea in the anaerobic rumen produce methane from CO₂ and hydrogen. They can only live in oxygen-free environments and occupy a niche in the digestive system.
items.markingKey: Context (Archaea in the anaerobic rumen produce methane from CO₂ and hydrogen.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: They can only live in oxygen-free environments and occupy a niche in the digestive system. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to obligate anaerobic metabolism.

items.stem: Lukas writes: "The niche of a species is the same as its habitat." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The habitat is where it lives; the niche is its full role, including resources used and interactions.
items.markingKey: The habitat is where it lives; the niche is its full role, including resources used and interactions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Classifying organisms by mode of nutrition is clear-cut."
items.answer: The categories are useful but nutrition is a spectrum, and mixotrophs show the boundary is not clear-cut.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: most organisms clearly fit autotroph or heterotroph categories; the categories reflect fundamental differences in metabolism. Arguments against: mixotrophs such as Euglena and carnivorous plants use both modes; some parasitic plants have lost photosynthesis partly or completely. Supported judgement: The categories are useful but nutrition is a spectrum, and mixotrophs show the boundary is not clear-cut.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "obligate aerobe"?
options: An organism that requires oxygen for respiration and cannot survive without it
Competition between individuals of different species for the same limited resources
A heterotroph that obtains nutrients by secreting digestive enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbing the products
A plant adapted to grow in saline (salty) conditions, such as mangroves and salt-marsh plants
items.answer: An organism that requires oxygen for respiration and cannot survive without it
items.markingKey: A. "obligate aerobe" is an organism that requires oxygen for respiration and cannot survive without it.

items.stem: Explain how the niche of a species is defined.
items.answer: The niche includes where the species lives (spatial habitat), when it is active, what it eats, its predators, competitors and parasites, and its tolerance of abiotic factors – its total role in the ecosystem.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The niche includes where the species lives (spatial habitat), when it is active, what it eats, its predators, competitors and parasites, and its tolerance of abiotic factors – its total role in the ecosystem. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition.
items.answer: Autotrophs make their own organic compounds from inorganic carbon (CO₂) using energy from light (photoautotrophs) or chemical reactions (chemoautotrophs); heterotrophs obtain carbon compounds from other organisms by ingestion, absorption (saprotrophs) or parasitism.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Autotrophs make their own organic compounds from inorganic carbon (CO₂) using energy from light (photoautotrophs) or chemical reactions (chemoautotrophs); heterotrophs obtain carbon compounds from other organisms by ingestion, absorption (saprotrophs) or parasitism. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A bacterium grows throughout a tube of nutrient broth but most densely at the top where oxygen is highest. What is it most likely to be?
options: an obligate aerobe that cannot grow lower down
items.answer: a facultative anaerobe
items.markingKey: C. Grows with or without O₂, better with it.

items.stem: "The niche of a species is the same as its habitat." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The habitat is where it lives; the niche is its full role, including resources used and interactions.
items.markingKey: The habitat is where it lives; the niche is its full role, including resources used and interactions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe the different modes of nutrition found in living organisms, with a named example of each.
items.answer: Photoautotrophs (plants, cyanobacteria), chemoautotrophs (vent archaea, nitrifying bacteria), holozoic heterotrophs (animals), saprotrophs (fungi, decomposer bacteria), mixotrophs (Euglena), parasites; obligate and facultative anaerobes (Clostridium, yeast); diversity of archaea.
items.markingKey: Photoautotrophs (plants, cyanobacteria), chemoautotrophs (vent archaea, nitrifying bacteria), holozoic heterotrophs (animals), saprotrophs (fungi, decomposer bacteria), mixotrophs (Euglena), parasites; obligate and facultative anaerobes (Clostridium, yeast); diversity of archaea.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Competition between individuals of different species for the same limited resources"?
items.answer: interspecific competition
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of interspecific competition.

items.stem: Why do monarch butterflies tolerate the toxins of milkweed?
options: They have evolved resistance and store the toxins as a defence against predators.
items.answer: They have evolved resistance and store the toxins as a defence against predators.
items.markingKey: D. Co-evolution of herbivore and plant.

items.stem: A student claims: "Prey adaptations evolve so that prey species are never eaten." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Adaptations increase the chance of survival of individuals; predation still occurs and predators also evolve.
items.markingKey: Adaptations increase the chance of survival of individuals; predation still occurs and predators also evolve. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe Gause’s Paramecium experiments (1934) and explain what it reveals about the competitive exclusion principle.
items.answer: P. aurelia and P. caudatum both grew alone, but in mixed culture P. caudatum died out. The species with greater growth rate on the shared resource excluded the other.
items.markingKey: Context (P. aurelia and P. caudatum both grew alone, but in mixed culture P. caudatum died out.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The species with greater growth rate on the shared resource excluded the other. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the competitive exclusion principle.

items.stem: Five warbler species feed in the same spruce trees in different zones of the canopy (MacArthur, 1958). What does this illustrate?
items.answer: resource partitioning reducing competition
items.markingKey: D. Different realised niches allow coexistence.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Competition is the main factor determining the structure of ecological communities."
items.answer: Competition is important, especially among similar species, but communities are structured by many interacting factors.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: classic experiments (Gause, Connell) show competition can exclude species and restrict niches; resource partitioning patterns are widespread. Arguments against: predation, disease and disturbance often keep populations below levels at which competition matters; mutualism and facilitation also shape communities. Supported judgement: Competition is important, especially among similar species, but communities are structured by many interacting factors.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "fundamental niche"?
options: The gradual change in distribution of species across a habitat in response to an environmental gradient, such as on a rocky shore
The range of values of an abiotic factor within which a species can survive, with an optimum range in which it thrives
The full range of conditions and resources a species could use in the absence of competitors
A heritable characteristic that increases an organism’s chance of survival and reproduction in its environment
items.answer: The full range of conditions and resources a species could use in the absence of competitors
items.markingKey: C. "fundamental niche" is the full range of conditions and resources a species could use in the absence of competitors.

items.stem: Distinguish between the realised niche and the fundamental niche.
items.answer: The fundamental niche is the potential range of conditions and resources without competitors; the realised niche is the actual, usually smaller, range occupied in the presence of competitors.

items.stem: Explain how adaptations of predators and prey result from natural selection.
items.answer: Prey with better defences (camouflage, speed, toxins) survive and reproduce more; predators with better hunting adaptations (speed, senses, teeth) catch more prey and reproduce more; this produces an evolutionary arms race in which both improve over generations.

items.stem: Explain how a species’ range of tolerance determines its distribution.
items.answer: Within the optimum range the population grows; towards the limits individuals are stressed and fewer survive or reproduce; beyond the limits they cannot survive; so the species occurs only where conditions fall within its tolerance range.

items.stem: With reference to red mangroves (Rhizophora mangle) in the Florida Everglades, explain how it illustrates adaptations to saline, anaerobic soils.
items.answer: They grow in tidal saline mud using prop roots and excluding salt at the roots. Specialised roots and salt control allow survival where few plants can grow.
items.markingKey: Context (They grow in tidal saline mud using prop roots and excluding salt at the roots.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Specialised roots and salt control allow survival where few plants can grow. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to adaptations to saline, anaerobic soils.

items.stem: Rafael writes: "A correlation between light intensity and fern abundance proves that light causes the distribution." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Correlation does not prove causation; other factors (e.g. soil moisture) may vary with light; experiments are needed to test causation.
items.markingKey: Correlation does not prove causation; other factors (e.g. soil moisture) may vary with light; experiments are needed to test causation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline one way in which methanogenic archaea in the rumen of cattle shows obligate anaerobic metabolism.
items.answer: Archaea in the anaerobic rumen produce methane from CO₂ and hydrogen. They can only live in oxygen-free environments and occupy a niche in the digestive system.
items.markingKey: Context (Archaea in the anaerobic rumen produce methane from CO₂ and hydrogen.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Abiotic factors are more important than biotic factors in determining the distribution of species."
items.answer: Abiotic factors determine where species could live (fundamental range), but biotic interactions often determine where they actually live.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: abiotic factors set the limits of tolerance (e.g. temperature limits of corals); biome patterns follow temperature and rainfall. Arguments against: competition, predation and disease often limit species within physically suitable areas; mutualists such as pollinators are needed for many plants. Supported judgement: Abiotic factors determine where species could live (fundamental range), but biotic interactions often determine where they actually live.

items.stem: "Classifying organisms by mode of nutrition is clear-cut." Discuss.
items.answer: The categories are useful but nutrition is a spectrum, and mixotrophs show the boundary is not clear-cut.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: most organisms clearly fit autotroph or heterotroph categories; the categories reflect fundamental differences in metabolism. Arguments against: mixotrophs such as Euglena and carnivorous plants use both modes; some parasitic plants have lost photosynthesis partly or completely. Supported judgement: The categories are useful but nutrition is a spectrum, and mixotrophs show the boundary is not clear-cut. items.stem: "Competition is the main factor determining the structure of ecological communities." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Competition is important, especially among similar species, but communities are structured by many interacting factors.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: classic experiments (Gause, Connell) show competition can exclude species and restrict niches; resource partitioning patterns are widespread. Arguments against: predation, disease and disturbance often keep populations below levels at which competition matters; mutualism and facilitation also shape communities. Supported judgement: Competition is important, especially among similar species, but communities are structured by many interacting factors. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

options: rolled leaves with sunken stomata, as in marram grass
items.answer: rolled leaves with sunken stomata, as in marram grass
items.markingKey: C. Reduces water loss in dry, windy dunes.

items.stem: Define the term "transect".
items.answer: A line across a habitat along which samples are taken at intervals to study changes in distribution with an environmental gradient

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A heterotroph that obtains nutrients by secreting digestive enzymes onto dead organic matter and absorbing the products"?
items.answer: saprotroph
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of saprotroph.

items.stem: Explain the competitive exclusion principle using a named example.
items.answer: Gause grew Paramecium aurelia and P. caudatum separately – both grew; together, competing for the same bacterial food, P. aurelia always outcompeted P. caudatum, which died out; two species cannot occupy the same niche indefinitely.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Gause grew Paramecium aurelia and P. caudatum separately – both grew; together, competing for the same bacterial food, P. aurelia always outcompeted P. caudatum, which died out; two species cannot occupy the same niche indefinitely. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: How does a thick waxy cuticle help xerophytes?
options: It absorbs water from the air.
It reduces water loss by evaporation from the leaf surface.
items.answer: It reduces water loss by evaporation from the leaf surface.
items.markingKey: B. Impermeable barrier.

items.stem: Why do similar biomes on different continents have similar adaptations but different species?
options: The same species spread across oceans.
Similar climates select for similar adaptations through convergent evolution.
items.answer: Similar climates select for similar adaptations through convergent evolution.
items.markingKey: B. E.g. cacti and euphorbias.

items.stem: Explain the difference between obligate anaerobes and facultative anaerobes.
items.answer: Obligate anaerobes cannot survive in oxygen; facultative anaerobes respire aerobically when oxygen is available but can switch to anaerobic metabolism when it is absent.
items.markingKey: Obligate anaerobes cannot survive in oxygen; facultative anaerobes respire aerobically when oxygen is available but can switch to anaerobic metabolism when it is absent. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between chemical defences of plants and physical defences of plants.
items.answer: Physical defences (spines, hairs, tough leaves) deter feeding mechanically; chemical defences (alkaloids, tannins, cyanogenic glycosides) make tissues toxic or unpalatable.
items.markingKey: Physical defences (spines, hairs, tough leaves) deter feeding mechanically; chemical defences (alkaloids, tannins, cyanogenic glycosides) make tissues toxic or unpalatable. items.stem: Explain how abiotic factors determine where a species can live.
items.answer: Each species has a range of tolerance for factors such as temperature, water, light, pH and salinity; it can only survive and reproduce where all factors are within its tolerance; so the distribution of abiotic factors limits its habitat.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Each species has a range of tolerance for factors such as temperature, water, light, pH and salinity; it can only survive and reproduce where all factors are within its tolerance; so the distribution of abiotic factors limits its habitat. items.stem: A student claims: "The niche of a species is the same as its habitat." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: The habitat is where it lives; the niche is its full role, including resources used and interactions.

items.answer: Adaptations increase the chance of survival of individuals; predation still occurs and predators also evolve.

items.stem: Plants on the windward side of a coastal cliff are shorter with smaller leaves than those on the sheltered side. Which is the best explanation?

Wind increases water loss and mechanical stress, selecting for smaller leaves and stature.

items.stem: Using Euglena gracilis in ponds as an example, explain mixotrophic nutrition.
items.answer: Euglena photosynthesises using chloroplasts in light and absorbs or ingests organic matter in darkness. Using both modes allows it to survive changing light conditions.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Transects are the most effective way to study species distribution in a habitat."
items.answer: Transects are best for gradients; other methods (random quadrats, mark–recapture, eDNA) suit other questions.

items.answer: (a) 22.6 individuals per 0.5 cm³ per day (b) -100 % (c) Slow initial increase, then rapid (exponential) growth, then levelling off at about 197 – sigmoid curve. (d) Both compete for the same limited bacterial food; P. aurelia grows faster/uses food more efficiently; P. caudatum declines and is excluded – competitive exclusion. (e) Competitive exclusion: two species with the same niche cannot coexist indefinitely. (f) Some food is consumed by P. caudatum before it is excluded. (g) Laboratory conditions are uniform and simple; in nature, habitat variation allows resource partitioning, and predators/disturbance may prevent exclusion.
